title: LNER's on-train video review flags a minor track fault near Retford a week after a driver-reported defect cost over 10,000 delay minutes, and engineers repair it overnight with zero delay minutes
summary: LNER reports that One Big Circle's Automated Intelligent Video Review (AIVR) system detected a minor track fault near Retford, which engineers repaired overnight with no delay to passengers.
account: LNER runs the Pantograph Damage Assessment System (PANDAS) and One Big Circle's Automated Intelligent Video Review (AIVR) on a number of its trains. They assess overhead line equipment and track and report potential damage to Network Rail. LNER states that AIVR, with underbody line-scanning cameras, was fitted to two bi-mode Azuma units in January 2026. In January 2026 a train driver in Cambridgeshire reported a track defect. It caused over 10,000 delay minutes, multiple cancellations and a full day of disruption. A week later the AIVR system identified a minor fault near Retford with the potential to become a larger issue. The Retford detection therefore came within weeks of installation. The exact day of the detection is not given. Engineers carried out an overnight repair with no delay to passengers and zero delay minutes. LNER announced the Retford result on 9 April 2026. The 10,000 delay minutes concern the separate Cambridgeshire event, and no source measures the delay saved at Retford. On 3 July 2026 the system flagged a snake as a track defect. New Civil Engineer's Tom Pashby reported the snake alert on 6 July 2026, and his article reproduces LNER's announcement of 9 April 2026. An LNER spokesperson said that the information is fed back to Network Rail to target areas for attention. A Network Rail spokesperson said that the snake would be raised automatically as standard practice.
purpose: AIVR is built to capture and analyze front-of-train video with machine learning. The aim is to find and fix track and lineside defects before they cause disruption.
system: Automated Intelligent Video Review (AIVR), using underbody line-scanning cameras on two LNER bi-mode Azuma trains
deployer: LNER (on-train cameras), with findings passed to Network Rail
